hints.text: Oh, come on. Everyone in Southie knows this. 1974. Courts, judges, buses. Think about what tore this neighborhood apart.
March 17th. Broadway. Been running since before your grandmother was born. Biggest parade in Boston.
Carson, L Street, M Street. Those are our beaches. That other one's up north. Way north.
Everyone knew who ran things around here. I never said his name. Nobody did. First name starts with W.
Crazy people who swim in the ocean year-round. L Street Bathhouse. They've been doing it since 1902.
Scorsese film. DiCaprio. Nicholson. Won Best Picture. Everyone in Hollywood wanted to play a gangster from Southie.
March 17th is convenient, isn't it? St. Patrick's Day AND Evacuation Day. State holiday. Banks close.
Castle Island has a fort. Named after a Revolutionary War hero. Think about independence.
We're not 'Townies' - that's Charlestown. Think about what you call THIS neighborhood.
Three floors. Three families. Working-class architecture. Hyphenated name.
The lanterns. Old North Church. 'One if by land, two if by sea.' Every schoolkid knows this.
Mike's Pastry. Been there since the 1940s. Modern came later. The cannoli war started early.
This neighborhood is OLD. Before the Common was a park. Early 1630s. Think about that.
Famous patriot. Silversmith. Midnight ride. His house is still here. You've probably walked past it.
Religious festivals all summer. They carry the saint through the streets. August is the big one. The Fishermen's Feast.
1919. January. Something sweet killed over 20 people. A tank burst. The cleanup took forever.
The copper on the State House dome. Paul Revere's company did that work. He wasn't just a rider.
Before my people came here, it was Irish. Before the Irish? Think about the original colonists.
The tunnel under the harbor. Named after a senator who served for decades. Tip of the hat.
They buried the Central Artery. The park on top is named after JFK's mother. Irish matriarch.
The wall in left field. Green as grass. Higher than you'd think. 37-something feet.
April 1912. Fenway opened. Same week something sank in the Atlantic. Big news week.
There's one red seat in the right field bleachers. Ted Williams hit one there. Longest ever at Fenway.
Before 2004, there was the Curse. Started when they sold a certain player to the Yankees. Big guy. Home runs.
The scoreboard on the Monster. No computers. Metal plates. Numbers by hand. Old school.
Teddy Ballgame. Greatest hitter ever. Played his whole career in Boston. Didn't go anywhere else.
The triangle in center field. Deepest part of the park. Over 400 feet. Weird angles.
One seat. Red. Right field. Marks where Ted Williams hit one 502 feet.
Eighth inning tradition. Neil Diamond song. 'So good! So good!' Everyone sings along.
The Green Monster has an official name. Named after the owner who built it. Not just 'the wall.'
The dome's been multiple things. Wood, copper, gold. Paul Revere's company did the copper. 1802.
The gaslights are real. Original 1800s. City maintains them. Protected by law.
One private street. Square-shaped name. Most exclusive address in Boston.
The architect who designed the State House. Famous name. Bulfinch. Half the important buildings in Boston.
African Meeting House. Underground Railroad. Free Black community. Important history up here.
The brick sidewalks are protected by law. Can't pave over them. Historic district rules.
The name tells you. 'Beacon.' What's a beacon for? Warning people. Think colonial times.
The Cheers bar is based on a real place. Different name in real life. Bull and Finch.
Look at the top of the State House. There's something up there. Pinecone shape. Symbol of something.
Some windows turned purple from the sun. Certain minerals in the old glass. Distinctive feature.
The battle wasn't actually on Bunker Hill. Different hill nearby. Starts with B too.
USS Constitution. Oldest commissioned warship still afloat. Cannonballs bounced off. Nickname is metal-related.
The monument has stairs inside. A lot of them. No elevator. 294 of them.
Charlestown was settled before Boston proper. Very early. 1620s. Think about that.
People from Charlestown have a nickname. Not Southies. Something about living in THE Town.
Famous order from the battle. Something about waiting. Eyes. Whites of them.
Navy Yard used to build ships. Closed in the 70s. Now it's condos and the Constitution.
There's the obelisk and a lodge. Lodge has the museum. Obelisk is just the monument.
Ben Affleck movie. Bank robbers. Nuns. Fenway Park heist. Set right here.
Constitution fires its cannons every day. Twice. Sunrise and sunset. Military tradition.
This entire neighborhood used to be water. Mudflats. Tidal marsh. The name tells you.
The library in Copley Square. Opened in 1895. First free public library in a major American city.
The brownstones all look similar. Victorian. French Academic influence. Planned neighborhood.
The streets go in alphabetical order. Start at the Public Garden. A, B, C, D...
Trinity Church. Beautiful building. The architect's style has his name in it. Richardsonian.
The tall glass building reflects Trinity Church. Famous photograph. Everyone calls it Hancock something.
The Boston Marathon finishes in Back Bay. Main street near the library. Starts with B.
They filled in Back Bay over decades. Started before the Civil War. Trainloads of gravel from Needham.
Grand boulevard with a walking path down the middle. 'Commonwealth' something. Modeled after the Champs-Elysees.
Where Back Bay meets Beacon Hill. Not the Common - the other one. Swan boats. Flower beds.
MIT moved to Cambridge in 1916. Before that, it was in Boston proper. Near Copley Square.
Harvard is the oldest university in America. 1630s. Before the country existed.
The statue in Harvard Yard. 'Three Lies.' Wrong date, wrong face, wrong title. Everyone rubs the shoe.
MIT started an AI lab in 1959. McCarthy and Minsky. Changed computing forever.
Cambridge had a different name before. 'Newtowne.' Then they renamed it after the English university.
Harvard's color. Not just 'red.' A specific shade. Sounds like a type of crime.
The bridge measured in unusual units. A student's body length. MIT prank from the 50s.
MIT students put things on the dome. Police cars, R2-D2. They call them 'hacks.'
First spreadsheet software. Before Excel. Before Lotus. Two-word name. Developed here.
Harvard Square has a T stop. What color line? Think geography. Charles River.
JFK wasn't born in Dorchester. Nearby, but not quite. Technically a different town. Starts with B.
Dorchester is the biggest neighborhood in Boston. About one-sixth of the whole city.
The housing style here. Three floors, three families. Has a hyphenated name.
Dorchester Heights. Washington put cannons there. British saw them and left. No battle.
Cape Verde has one of its biggest American communities here. Very diverse neighborhood.
Locals abbreviate the name. Three letters. Starts with D. We don't say the whole thing.
Dorchester was its own town before. Boston annexed it. Happened around 1870.
Famous coffee chain started nearby. Quincy, technically. 'America runs on' this brand.
Every June, there's a parade. Dot Day. Celebrating the neighborhood.
Oldest wooden building in Boston is here. Built in the 1600s. Family name starts with B.
The Freedom Trail has a specific number of stops. More than a dozen. Most people lose count.
Faneuil Hall started as a marketplace. Ground floor for goods. Upstairs for meetings.
Boston Massacre. Outside the OLD State House. King Street, now State Street.
On top of Faneuil Hall. Weathervane. Not an eagle, not a whale. An insect. Green.
Old North Church. 'One if by land.' Which neighborhood is it IN? Not Downtown. Think geography.
Boston Common. Oldest public park in America. 1630s. Before anything else.
Revolutionary heroes in one cemetery. Starts with G. Revere, Adams, Hancock - all there.
The Tea Party. How many chests? Exact number. Over 300. Under 400.
Before they threw the tea, they gathered somewhere. Meeting house. 'Old South' something.
The big market hall next to Faneuil. Named after a mayor. Starts with Q.
Big Dig. Most expensive highway project ever. Started at $2 billion. Ended at... much more.
They buried the Central Artery. I-93. The park on top is named after JFK's mother.
This used to be industrial. Warehouses. Fishing. South Boston Waterfront. Nobody lived here.
There's a museum where you reenact the Tea Party. Throw tea in the harbor. Replica ships.
Tunnel to the airport. Named after a baseball player. Ted Williams. About 1.6 miles.
The ICA moved here and changed everything. Art museum. Mid-2000s. Building over the water.
Massive convention center here. BCEC. Biggest in New England.
Critics say this neighborhood is missing something. Too expensive. Not enough diversity.
Big companies here now. Vertex Pharmaceuticals. Amazon has a presence too.
The Seaport borders water. Boston Harbor. Not the river.

southie.text: 1974. I was sixteen. The whole neighborhood went crazy. Judge Garrity made a ruling about schools. Suddenly everyone was throwing rocks at buses. Changed everything.
The parade. Broadway. March 17th. I marched in it fifty years straight. Never missed one until I got sick.
Carson, L Street, M Street. Our beaches. Revere's up north. Different world. Swam at all of ours in January once.
There was one man who ran everything in Southie. I never met him - at least, that's what I told people. Everyone knew. Nobody said it.
L Street Brownies. Crazy bastards swim in the ocean in January. Been doing it since 1902. I did it once. Never again.

north_end.text: Old North Church. Two lanterns. 'One if by land, two if by sea.' Every Bostonian knows this. Paul Revere. Midnight ride.
Mike's Pastry. 1946. Modern opened later. Don't let anyone tell you different. I knew the original Mike.
Oldest residential neighborhood in Boston. Settled in the 1630s. Before the Common was even a park.
Paul Revere. Silversmith. Patriot. His house is still standing in the North End. Walked past it a thousand times.
The feasts. They carry the saint through the streets. Pin money to it. The Fishermen's Feast in August. Beautiful tradition.

fenway.text: The Green Monster. 37 feet tall. Looks taller when you're standing at home plate. Changes everything about left field.
April 1912. Fenway opened. Same week the Titanic went down. Both made headlines.
Section 42, Row 37, Seat 21. Red seat. Ted Williams hit one there in 1946. 502 feet. Unbelievable.
The Curse. Started in 1918 when they sold Ruth to the Yankees. Ended in 2004. I cried that night.
Manual scoreboard. No electricity. They slide numbers in and out by hand. Been that way for over a century.

beacon_hill.text: The dome was wood first. Then copper - Revere did that. Then gold leaf since 1874. Three versions.
Gas lamps. Real gas. Been there since the 1800s. City maintains them. Part of what makes the Hill special.
Louisburg Square. Private street. Residents own it. Most exclusive address in Boston. Money has money there.
Charles Bulfinch. Designed the State House. Half the important buildings in early Boston. The man was a genius.
African Meeting House. Underground Railroad. Free Black community on Beacon Hill. Important history most people don't know.

charlestown.text: Bunker Hill battle was actually fought on Breed's Hill. They got the name wrong. Happens sometimes.
Old Ironsides. USS Constitution. Cannonballs bounced off the hull. That's where the nickname came from.
294 steps in the monument. I climbed them once. Once was enough. No elevator. My knees still remember.
Charlestown was settled in 1628. Before Boston proper. One of the oldest places in all of Massachusetts.
Townies. That's what they call people from Charlestown. Different from Southies. Don't mix them up.

back_bay.text: Back Bay was a swamp. Tidal flats. They filled it in with gravel starting in the 1850s. Every building sits on landfill.
Boston Public Library. 1895. The building in Copley Square. Murals inside by Sargent. Free to see. Free to use.
Victorian brownstones. French Academic style. Rich people wanted it to look like Paris. It kind of does.
Arlington, Berkeley, Clarendon, Dartmouth, Exeter, Fairfield, Gloucester, Hereford. Alphabetical. Easy to remember.
H.H. Richardson. Trinity Church. Richardsonian Romanesque - they named a whole style after him. Died at 47.

cambridge.text: MIT moved from Back Bay to Cambridge in 1916. Crossed the Charles River. Best decision they ever made.
Harvard. 1636. Oldest college in America. Before there was an America. Think about that.
Statue of Three Lies. Wrong date, wrong face, wrong title. John Harvard wasn't the founder. Everyone rubs the shoe anyway.
MIT AI Lab. 1959. McCarthy, Minsky. They thought machines could think. Turns out they were right.
Newtowne. That's what Cambridge was called before 1638. Then they renamed it after the English university. Ambitious.

dorchester.text: JFK was born in Brookline, not Dorchester. Common mistake. 83 Beals Street. You can visit the house.
Dorchester is huge. One-sixth of Boston. Six square miles. People don't realize how big it is.
Triple-deckers. Three floors, three families. That's how working people built this neighborhood. Smart design.
Dorchester Heights. Washington put cannons up there. British looked up, saw them, and left. March 17, 1776.
Cape Verde. One of the biggest Cape Verdean communities in America is right here in Dorchester. Beautiful people.

downtown.text: Sixteen stops on the Freedom Trail. Most tourists quit after ten. I walked all sixteen. Every year. Paid my respects.
Faneuil Hall was a marketplace first. Ground floor for goods, upstairs for meetings. The liberty stuff came later.
Boston Massacre. Outside the Old State House. March 5, 1770. Crispus Attucks was the first to fall.
Grasshopper weathervane on Faneuil Hall. Shem Drowne made it in 1742. During the Revolution, it was a loyalty test.
Old North Church is in the North End. Not Downtown. Different neighborhood. Common mistake.

seaport.text: Big Dig. Almost fifteen billion dollars. Started at two billion. Cost overruns, corruption. But it worked. Mostly.
They buried the Central Artery. I-93. Rose Kennedy Greenway on top now. Named after JFK's mother.
Used to be warehouses and fishing. South Boston Waterfront. Nobody wanted to live there. Look at it now.
Tea Party Ships museum. You can throw tea in the harbor. Every tourist does it. I did it three times.
Ted Williams Tunnel. About 1.6 miles. Part of the Big Dig. Used to drive through just to feel like I was underwater.

gauntletSullyReactions.text: Alright, I'll give you this one. But only one. You're on your own after this.
Halfway there, kid. Keep your head in it.
Last one. Everything you've learned comes down to this.
Three in a row. You're finding your rhythm now.
Five straight. Maybe you did learn something from me after all.
Shake it off. Plenty of questions left.
